system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 6: MODULE 4 - ARRANGING FOR SOLO GUITAR

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 6 — MODULE 4 - ARRANGING FOR SOLO GUITAR

_Pages 181-240._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## diads as octave alternative

> This is an alternative approach to using octaves and is a softer but richer sound, which sounds very
> authentic in the jazz guitar tradition.

**Significance (p. 181).** Defines the sonic rationale for choosing diads over octaves in solo jazz guitar arranging.

## walking bass construction

> Place the root on beat 1 of each bar:

**Significance (p. 184).** States the foundational rule for starting a walking bassline, anchoring all subsequent steps.

## walking bass beat 4 approach

> Now add either a diatonic or chromatic note on beat 4, above or below the following root note:

**Significance (p. 185).** Introduces the approach-note concept on beat 4 as the second step in building a walking bass.

## walking bass inner notes

> To complete your walking bassline, you just need to add two more notes in between the root note of
> beat 1, and the approach note of beat 4.
>
> These can be any of the following:
>
> e Diatonic notes from the scale of the given key.
> e Chromatic notes, or
> e Arpeggios.

**Significance (p. 185).** Completes the four-step walking bass construction method by specifying the three note-type options for beats 2 and 3.

## walking bass shell voicings

> Now you can add shell voicings on the root notes on each bar.
>
> It’s good to mix up playing them on the downbeat and on the ‘& of 1’ to create variety:

**Significance (p. 186).** Explains how to layer chord voicings onto the walking bass and gives a rhythmic variation rule for keeping the texture fresh.

## walking bass melodic role

> Notice how the walking bass is used to fill out sections where there is a long-held melody note — this
> helps keep the drive and swing moving.

**Significance (p. 187).** States the functional principle for when to deploy walking bass within a melody arrangement.

## passing chords diatonic option

> Option 1 (Diatonic Notes Only) Use Your Chord Dictionary
>
> If you see extra notes you want to harmonize in the melody, and the notes are diatonic, you already
> have what you need from this course.
>
> Simply use voicings from the chord dictionary provided in Appendix 1 to harmonize the melody at
> additional points.

**Significance (p. 196).** Defines the first passing-chord strategy and directs the student to the chord dictionary as the tool for diatonic harmonization.

## chromatic approach chords

> In this case, you can use a voicing on the note being approached, then play the same voicing one fret
> away for the approach note in the melody:

**Significance (p. 197).** Gives the mechanical rule for constructing a chromatic approach chord — same voicing shape moved one fret.

## tritone substitution definition

> Tritone substitution is the process of substituting one chord for another a tritone away.

**Significance (p. 214).** Provides the concise, definitional statement of tritone substitution.

## tritone as split octave

> This is why a tritone interval is sometimes referred to as a split octave - as the tritone interval splits
> an octave precisely in half:

**Significance (p. 215).** Explains the symmetric interval property that makes tritone substitution work.

## guide tones swap in tritone sub

> C7 has E as the 3rd and Bb as the 7th.
> F#7 has E as the 7th and A# (which is the same as Bb) as the 3rd.
>
> The guide tones have essentially swapped places between these two chords.
>
> Because the two chords have those 3rd and 7th as common tones, they can be substituted for
> one another.

**Significance (p. 216).** Explains the voice-leading mechanism — shared guide tones — that makes tritone substitution harmonically valid.

## tritone substitution rule

> Tritone Substitution Rule - You can replace any chord with another whose root is a tritone
> away from the root of the original chord.

**Significance (p. 220).** States the practical application rule for tritone substitution in a single, memorable sentence.

## substitution use in solo guitar

> When it comes to solo guitar, you have the freedom to do these kinds of substitutions liberally as it’s
> just you on stage.

**Significance (p. 220).** Clarifies the performance context that permits free use of substitutions — solo setting vs. ensemble.

## relative substitution rule

> Rule: you can replace the I chord of a key with the vi chord of the key.

**Significance (p. 224).** States the relative substitution rule in its most compact, actionable form.

## chord iii substitution rule

> Rule: you can substitute a major chord for chord iii of its key.

**Significance (p. 225).** Provides the second major-to-minor substitution rule.

## chord addition defined

> This process is referred to as chord addition — adding extra chords to the harmony.

**Significance (p. 228).** Names and defines the technique of inserting substitution chords to expand the harmonic rhythm.

## minor for dominant substitution rule

> You can use a minor 7 chord from the 5th of any dominant chord (which is like using the iim7 that
> belongs to the dominant chord).
>
> For example: an F7 chord’s 5th interval is C. So you could play Cm7 over F7 to get an interesting
> sound.

**Significance (p. 230).** States and illustrates the minor-for-dominant substitution rule with a concrete numerical example.

## ii–V interchangeability

> Joe Pass would often mention that the ii and the V chord can be interchanged with one another, and
> this is the reason - they are very similar in their construction.

**Significance (p. 230).** Cites the theoretical basis for the ii/V substitution by attributing it to Joe Pass.
